kernels.definition: Metamorphic rock forms when heat, pressure, and fluids change a preexisting parent rock (the protolith) in the solid state, without melting it.

definitionAnchor.quote: Metamorphic rocks are created when heat, pressure, and/or fluids change preexisting rocks

facts.text: Metamorphism changes a solid rock's composition and texture without the mineral crystals melting.

anchor.quote: Metamorphism occurs when solid rock changes composition and/or texture without mineral crystals melting

facts.text: The starting rock that undergoes metamorphism is called the parent rock, or protolith.

anchor.quote: are called the parent rock, or protolith

facts.text: Directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes, producing foliation.

anchor.quote: Foliation is a term used that describes minerals lined up in planes

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §6.1 Metamorphism and metamorphic rocks

kernels.definition: The rock cycle describes how Earth's three rock families — igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic — form and continually transform into one another through geologic processes.

definitionAnchor.quote: the process of changing rocks on Earth into different forms, namely igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic

facts.text: The rock cycle describes the major Earth materials, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other.

anchor.quote: describes the major materials that comprise the Earth, the processes that form them, and how they relate to each other

facts.text: Igneous rock forms when liquid rock freezes solid; lithified sediment becomes sedimentary rock; pre-existing rock can transform into metamorphic rock.

anchor.quote: Igneous rock is formed when liquid rock freezes into a solid rock

facts.text: If conditions melt the rocks into magma, the cycle begins anew with new igneous rocks.

anchor.quote: the rock cycle begins anew with the creation of new rocks

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §4 The rock cycle

kernels.definition: Earth is layered into a thin outer crust, a thick rocky mantle, and a metallic core; the upper mantle's asthenosphere is solid rock that flows slowly by convection.

definitionAnchor.quote: The outermost chemical layer and the one we currently reside on is the crust

facts.text: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core.

anchor.quote: The mantle sits below the crust and above the core

facts.text: The core has both liquid and solid layers and is made mostly of iron and nickel.

anchor.quote: The core of the Earth has both liquid and solid layers and consists mostly of iron, nickel, and possibly some oxygen

facts.text: The asthenosphere is mechanically weak and flows by convection currents driven by the core's heat.

anchor.quote: this layer moves and flows due to convection currents created by heat coming from the earth's core

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.1 Earth's interior

kernels.definition: Plate tectonics holds that Earth's rigid lithosphere is broken into plates that move over the ductile asthenosphere; most geologic action occurs at their three kinds of boundaries.

definitionAnchor.quote: Plate boundaries are where most of Earth's geologic action occurs

facts.text: At divergent boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created.

anchor.quote: At divergent boundaries, sometimes called constructive boundaries, lithospheric plates move away from each other

facts.text: At convergent boundaries, two or more plates move toward each other and lithosphere is destroyed.

anchor.quote: Convergent boundaries, also called destructive boundaries, are places where two or more plates move toward each other

facts.text: At a transform boundary, plates slide horizontally past each other.

anchor.quote: A transform boundary is where the lithospheric plates slide past each other in the horizontal plane

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §2.4 Plate boundaries

kernels.definition: An earthquake releases stored elastic energy when rock slips along a fault; the energy travels outward as seismic waves, including fast compressional P waves and slower shear S waves.

definitionAnchor.quote: Earthquakes are felt at the surface of the Earth when energy is released by blocks of rock sliding past each other, i.e. faulting has occurred

facts.text: Elastic rebound theory explains earthquakes: stored energy is released and the broken rock springs back toward its original position.

anchor.quote: The release of seismic energy is explained by the elastic rebound theory

facts.text: P waves are the fastest body waves and move by compression, like sound through air, so they travel through solids, liquids, and gases.

anchor.quote: enabling them to travel through solids, liquids, plasma, and gases

facts.text: S waves are slower shear waves restricted to lateral motion, so they travel only through solids, never liquids.

anchor.quote: S waves can only travel through solids but not liquids, plasma, or gases

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §9.1 Earthquakes and seismic waves

kernels.definition: Geologic time spans the roughly 4.5-billion-year history of Earth; relative dating orders events by which is older or younger, while absolute dating assigns numerical ages in years.

definitionAnchor.quote: Relative dating is the process of determining if one rock or geologic event is older or younger than another, without knowing their specific ages

facts.text: Absolute (numerical) dating assigns specific ages in years to mineral grains within a rock.

anchor.quote: Absolute dating assigns specific time units, in this case years, to mineral grains within a rock

facts.text: By the principle of superposition, in an undisturbed sequence the bottom layers are oldest and the upper layers younger.

anchor.quote: the layers on the bottom are the oldest, and the layers above them are younger

facts.text: By original horizontality, sediments and lava flows are laid down horizontally, so tilted layers were disturbed after deposition.
The Earth is about 4.54 billion years old, and this vastness of geologic time allowed life to evolve.

anchor.quote: The current estimate for the age of the Earth is 4.54 billion years

attribution: An Introduction to Geology (opengeology.org), §7.1 Relative dating and geologic time

mcItems.q: A quartzite layer is described as having formed when heat, pressure, and fluids changed an earlier sandstone body without melting. What is that earlier sandstone body called?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is protolith, because it is the starting rock that undergoes metamorphism. The other plausible distractor is metamorphic band, but that describes the product’s fabric, not the original parent rock.

mcItems.q: A shale sample shows mineral crystals lined up in planes after strong directed stress, but the rock did not melt. Which process best explains the aligned texture?
mcItems.ex: Directed stress causing foliation is correct because directed stress aligns mineral crystals into planes in solid rock. The most plausible misconception is rapid cooling from lava, but that involves an igneous process and does not explain planar crystal alignment in a preexisting rock.

keyTerms.df: A preexisting rock that becomes the starting material for metamorphism.
keyTerms.eg: Sandstone is the protolith of quartzite.
keyTerms.mi: It means the new metamorphic rock itself.
keyTerms.cx: The protolith is the parent rock; the metamorphic rock is the altered product.

keyTerms.df: A planar texture created when directed stress aligns mineral crystals.
keyTerms.eg: A metamorphic rock with visible mineral bands formed under directed stress.
keyTerms.mi: Any banded rock must be foliation, including layers deposited in water.
keyTerms.cx: Foliation is produced by stress-driven crystal alignment, not by sediment deposition.

mcItems.ex: The correct choice is protolith, because it is the starting rock that undergoes metamorphism. The other plausible distractor is metamorphic band, but that describes the product’s fabric, not the original parent rock.

mcItems.q: A buried layer of loose sediment becomes a hard rock after compaction and cementation. Which rock-family change is described?
op: The sediment is lithified into sedimentary rock.
The sediment melts into magma and then cools.
The sediment is squeezed into metamorphic rock.
The sediment freezes into igneous rock.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is lithified sediment becoming sedimentary rock. The other choices describe different rock-cycle steps: melting to magma, changing by metamorphism, or freezing from liquid rock.

mcItems.q: A volcano produces magma, and later that molten material cools and solidifies. What rock-family result follows?
op: It becomes metamorphic rock through heat and pressure.
It becomes sedimentary rock by cementing layers.
It becomes igneous rock when liquid rock freezes solid.
It returns to magma after being lithified.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is igneous rock forming when liquid rock freezes solid. A common misconception is to treat any new rock as sedimentary or metamorphic, but those require lithified sediment or pre-existing rock altered by different processes.

keyTerms.df: A rock made when liquid rock solidifies into a new solid form.
keyTerms.eg: Magma cooling after a volcanic eruption can form igneous rock.
keyTerms.mi: Any rock formed at Earth’s surface is igneous.
keyTerms.cx: Surface formation alone does not make a rock igneous; the defining step is freezing from liquid rock.

keyTerms.df: A linked set of processes that forms Earth’s major rock families and changes them into one another.
keyTerms.eg: Sediment can lithify into sedimentary rock, and melted rock can later freeze into new igneous rock.
keyTerms.mi: The cycle is a one-way path from one rock type to the next.
keyTerms.cx: The cycle is continual, with rock families transforming back and forth through geologic processes.

mcItems.q: Which layer lies below the crust and above the core?
mcItems.ex: The mantle is the layer between the crust and the core. A common misconception is to pick the asthenosphere, but that is a mechanically weak part of the upper mantle rather than a separate layer between crust and core.

mcItems.q: What best describes the asthenosphere?
op: A rigid surface shell that does not move
A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle that flows slowly by convection
A metallic region made mostly of iron and nickel
A liquid layer above the crust
mcItems.ex: The asthenosphere is solid rock that is mechanically weak and flows slowly by convection. A plausible misconception is to call it liquid, but the source says it is solid rock, not a liquid layer.

keyTerms.df: The thick rocky layer that sits beneath the crust and above the core.
keyTerms.eg: The mantle is the layer identified when comparing rock structure below the crust.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the core because both are deep Earth layers.
keyTerms.cx: The mantle is distinct from the core; the source places it between the crust and the core.

mcItems.q: A geologist maps a ridge where new oceanic crust is forming as two plates move apart. Which boundary best fits the evidence?
mcItems.ex: Divergent boundary is correct because the plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created there. A common misconception is choosing a convergent boundary, but that would require plates moving toward each other and lithosphere being destroyed instead.

mcItems.q: Along a fault, two plates are observed moving sideways past one another with little direct creation or destruction of lithosphere. What boundary is this?
mcItems.ex: Transform boundary is correct because plates slide horizontally past each other. The tempting misconception is subduction or another convergent setting, but convergent boundaries involve plates moving toward each other and lithosphere being destroyed.

keyTerms.df: A plate boundary where neighboring plates move away from each other and fresh lithosphere forms.
keyTerms.eg: Mid-ocean ridge spreading that adds new oceanic crust.
keyTerms.mi: It is a place where crust is mainly consumed.
keyTerms.cx: Correct it by linking separation with creation of new lithosphere, not destruction.

keyTerms.df: A boundary where plates move sideways past one another.
keyTerms.eg: A fault zone with horizontal plate motion.
keyTerms.mi: It must always build or destroy lithosphere.
keyTerms.cx: Correct it by focusing on sideways motion; creation and destruction are not the defining feature.

mcItems.q: Which event best describes what happens when an earthquake starts along a fault?
op: Stored elastic energy is released and seismic waves radiate outward
Magma cools and hardens into new crust
Sediment is compacted into a denser layer
The ground bends slowly without any sudden energy release
mcItems.ex: Correct: an earthquake begins when stored elastic energy is released as rock slips along a fault, sending seismic waves outward. A common misconception is that earthquakes are caused by slow bending or by rock forming processes, but those describe different geologic changes, not the sudden release.

mcItems.q: A seismic wave that is the fastest body wave and can move through solids, liquids, and gases is which one?
mcItems.ex: Correct: P waves are the fastest body waves and travel by compression through solids, liquids, and gases. The most plausible mistake is choosing S wave, but S waves are slower shear waves and can travel only through solids.

keyTerms.df: A process in which strained rock suddenly releases stored energy and springs back toward its original shape after fault movement.
keyTerms.eg: After a fault slips in an earthquake, the surrounding rock rebounds toward its earlier position.
keyTerms.mi: Earthquakes happen because rock slowly melts and then hardens again.
keyTerms.cx: The theory explains earthquakes as the release of stored elastic energy, not as melting or cooling.

keyTerms.df: A slower seismic body wave that moves by shear, with motion restricted to side-to-side or lateral movement.
keyTerms.eg: An S wave passing through bedrock can shake the ground sideways.
keyTerms.mi: S waves travel through every material because all waves do.
keyTerms.cx: S waves travel only through solids and never through liquids.

mcItems.q: A geologist studies an undisturbed stack of sedimentary rock layers in a canyon. Which inference is best supported about the layer positions?
op: All layers formed at the same time
The oldest layer must be tilted
mcItems.ex: The lowest layer formed first in an undisturbed sequence, which is the principle of superposition. A common misconception is that the top layer must be oldest because it is easiest to see, but superposition says the bottom layers are older and the upper layers younger.

mcItems.q: A lab reports that zircon grains in a rock are 2.1 billion years old. What kind of dating does this result represent?

mcItems.q: What best describes how metamorphic rock forms?
op: A preexisting rock changes in the solid state under heat, pressure, and fluids.
A rock melts completely and then cools into a new texture.
A starting rock is called a protolith before any change begins.
Directed stress aligns crystals into planes and always makes melting occur.
mcItems.ex: Heat, pressure, and fluids change a solid protolith without melting it. Melting is the misconception; metamorphism keeps the rock solid.

mcItems.q: A quartzite layer is described as having formed when heat, pressure, and fluids changed an earlier sandstone body without melting. What is that earlier sandstone body called?
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is protolith, because it is the starting rock that undergoes metamorphism. The other plausible distractor is metamorphic band, but that describes the product’s fabric, not the original parent rock.

mcItems.q: A buried layer of loose sediment becomes a hard rock after compaction and cementation. Which rock-family change is described?
op: The sediment is lithified into sedimentary rock.
The sediment melts into magma and then cools.
The sediment is squeezed into metamorphic rock.
The sediment freezes into igneous rock.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is lithified sediment becoming sedimentary rock. The other choices describe different rock-cycle steps: melting to magma, changing by metamorphism, or freezing from liquid rock.

mcItems.q: A volcano produces magma, and later that molten material cools and solidifies. What rock-family result follows?
op: It becomes metamorphic rock through heat and pressure.
It becomes sedimentary rock by cementing layers.
It becomes igneous rock when liquid rock freezes solid.
It returns to magma after being lithified.
mcItems.ex: The correct choice is igneous rock forming when liquid rock freezes solid. A common misconception is to treat any new rock as sedimentary or metamorphic, but those require lithified sediment or pre-existing rock altered by different processes.

keyTerms.df: A rock made when liquid rock solidifies into a new solid form.
keyTerms.eg: Magma cooling after a volcanic eruption can form igneous rock.
keyTerms.mi: Any rock formed at Earth’s surface is igneous.
keyTerms.cx: Surface formation alone does not make a rock igneous; the defining step is freezing from liquid rock.

keyTerms.df: A linked set of processes that forms Earth’s major rock families and changes them into one another.
keyTerms.eg: Sediment can lithify into sedimentary rock, and melted rock can later freeze into new igneous rock.
keyTerms.mi: The cycle is a one-way path from one rock type to the next.
keyTerms.cx: The cycle is continual, with rock families transforming back and forth through geologic processes.

mcItems.q: Which layer lies below the crust and above the core?
mcItems.ex: The mantle is the layer between the crust and the core. A common misconception is to pick the asthenosphere, but that is a mechanically weak part of the upper mantle rather than a separate layer between crust and core.

mcItems.q: What best describes the asthenosphere?
op: A rigid surface shell that does not move
A mechanically weak part of the upper mantle that flows slowly by convection
A metallic region made mostly of iron and nickel
A liquid layer above the crust
mcItems.ex: The asthenosphere is solid rock that is mechanically weak and flows slowly by convection. A plausible misconception is to call it liquid, but the source says it is solid rock, not a liquid layer.

keyTerms.df: The thick rocky layer that sits beneath the crust and above the core.
keyTerms.eg: The mantle is the layer identified when comparing rock structure below the crust.
keyTerms.mi: It is the same as the core because both are deep Earth layers.
keyTerms.cx: The mantle is distinct from the core; the source places it between the crust and the core.

keyTerms.df: A mechanically weak zone of the upper mantle that moves slowly by convection.
keyTerms.eg: Students may use the asthenosphere to explain slow rock flow beneath the lithosphere.
keyTerms.mi: It is a fully liquid layer.
keyTerms.cx: The source describes it as solid rock that flows slowly, not as liquid.

mcItems.q: A geologist maps a ridge where new oceanic crust is forming as two plates move apart. Which boundary best fits the evidence?
mcItems.ex: Divergent boundary is correct because the plates move away from each other and new lithosphere is created there. A common misconception is choosing a convergent boundary, but that would require plates moving toward each other and lithosphere being destroyed instead.

mcItems.q: Along a fault, two plates are observed moving sideways past one another with little direct creation or destruction of lithosphere. What boundary is this?
mcItems.ex: Transform boundary is correct because plates slide horizontally past each other. The tempting misconception is subduction or another convergent setting, but convergent boundaries involve plates moving toward each other and lithosphere being destroyed.

keyTerms.df: A plate boundary where neighboring plates move away from each other and fresh lithosphere forms.
keyTerms.eg: Mid-ocean ridge spreading that adds new oceanic crust.
keyTerms.mi: It is a place where crust is mainly consumed.
keyTerms.cx: Correct it by linking separation with creation of new lithosphere, not destruction.

keyTerms.df: A boundary where plates move sideways past one another.
keyTerms.eg: A fault zone with horizontal plate motion.
keyTerms.mi: It must always build or destroy lithosphere.
keyTerms.cx: Correct it by focusing on sideways motion; creation and destruction are not the defining feature.

mcItems.q: Which event best describes what happens when an earthquake starts along a fault?
op: Stored elastic energy is released and seismic waves radiate outward
Magma cools and hardens into new crust
Sediment is compacted into a denser layer
The ground bends slowly without any sudden energy release
mcItems.ex: Correct: an earthquake begins when stored elastic energy is released as rock slips along a fault, sending seismic waves outward. A common misconception is that earthquakes are caused by slow bending or by rock forming processes, but those describe different geologic changes, not the sudden release.

mcItems.q: A seismic wave that is the fastest body wave and can move through solids, liquids, and gases is which one?
mcItems.ex: Correct: P waves are the fastest body waves and travel by compression through solids, liquids, and gases. The most plausible mistake is choosing S wave, but S waves are slower shear waves and can travel only through solids.

keyTerms.df: A process in which strained rock suddenly releases stored energy and springs back toward its original shape after fault movement.
keyTerms.eg: After a fault slips in an earthquake, the surrounding rock rebounds toward its earlier position.
keyTerms.mi: Earthquakes happen because rock slowly melts and then hardens again.
keyTerms.cx: The theory explains earthquakes as the release of stored elastic energy, not as melting or cooling.

keyTerms.df: A slower seismic body wave that moves by shear, with motion restricted to side-to-side or lateral movement.
keyTerms.eg: An S wave passing through bedrock can shake the ground sideways.
keyTerms.mi: S waves travel through every material because all waves do.
keyTerms.cx: S waves travel only through solids and never through liquids.
